content: Invasive pneumococcal disease is a condition associated with high mortality rates. Many countries have incorporated routine pneumococcal vaccination into their childhood immunization programs to address this issue. Although pneumococcal disease is relatively rare in individuals with cystic fibrosis, vaccination against pneumococcus may provide some level of protection against pulmonary exacerbations caused by this pathogen. In both the United States and the United Kingdom, pneumococcal vaccination is currently recommended for all children and adults diagnosed with cystic fibrosis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccines in reducing morbidity among individuals with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register. This register includes references obtained from extensive electronic database searches, as well as manual searches of relevant journals and conference proceedings. Additionally, pharmaceutical manufacturers of both polysaccharide and conjugate pneumococcal vaccines were contacted for relevant data. The most recent search was conducted on June 27, 2016. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared pneumococcal vaccination (using either polysaccharide or conjugate vaccines) with non-vaccination or placebo in children or adults with cystic fibrosis. However, no relevant trials meeting these criteria were identified. As a result, this review does not include any trials, and no conclusions can be drawn regarding the efficacy of routine pneumococcal vaccination in reducing morbidity or mortality in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Given that many countries have already incorporated pneumococcal vaccination into their standard childhood immunization schedules, it is unlikely that future randomized controlled trials will be conducted to address this question. Instead, rigorously designed epidemiological studies may provide an alternative means to assess the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccination in reducing morbidity and mortality in this population.
